job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Hana Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the payroll team at a factory that makes car parts, on the edge of Coventry. There are four of us, and we pay about 900 people every two weeks, so a lot of my day is checking hours, fixing errors and answering the shop-floor guys who think their overtime is missing. On Saturdays I go to my parents' grocery shop and do their books at the back counter. I live in a rented house with two cousins, and I pay my loan and a share of the rent before I do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit overblown. At work I'd say there's always been a new system promising to do everything, and the pay still goes wrong on the odd Friday. At home I'd say it to my mum, who'd tell me to be grateful for a steady job and not to fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm mostly fine, because the factory has to pay people and somebody has to deal with the errors. What worries me is my own money. My loan is big, I've got less than a month in the bank, and the pay for my job is low, so every bill feels loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the payroll carefully and try the team's new checking tool when it's ready, because I use these things now and then. I'd put 100 a month into the loan and keep helping at my parents' shop on Saturdays. I'd ask my manager, Mrs Grewal, to add me to the pension-reporting work, which is trickier and pays more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite settled. A bit like a Sunday afternoon: nothing urgent, but you're aware Monday is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when somebody's pay is wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The man comes to my desk, red in the face, saying he's been short by 40. Nine times out of ten it's a code, not a mistake. I explain it kindly and show him on the screen. They trust me because I don't speak to them as if they're stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family say about you working in an office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're proud, which is lovely, but there's pressure too. I'm the first in the family to go to university and everyone's watching. If I fail they'd say nothing, but I'd feel it for a year.

say: I'd say it's a bit **overblown**, since the pay still goes wrong on some Fridays.
I'd tell my mum, who'd say be **grateful** and don't fuss.
think: The factory has to pay people, so the job feels **safe**; my money is the worry.
A big loan, under a month saved and low pay make every **bill** loud.
do: Try the team's new **checking tool** when it's ready.
Put **100** a month into the loan and help at my parents' shop on Saturdays.
Ask Mrs Grewal (my manager) for the trickier **pension reporting** work.
feel: Quite **settled**, like a Sunday afternoon with Monday coming.

fieldNote: Her **job** feels safe, but loan and rent keep her uneasy.

She wants trickier work, a sign of steady, planned ambition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change office jobs a lot, and that workers need to be involved from the start. At work I'd ask the company to say what it's changing before it does it. At home I'd say it's like the supermarket self-checkouts, which didn't close the shops but changed the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think payroll is exactly the sort of work that gets done by software. Hours, rules, errors, all of it is thinking work with fixed rules. Four of us pay 900 people. I could see it being two of us in three years, and I'm the youngest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new system better than anyone and offer to train the others, so I'm useful. I'd ask to move toward the employee relations side, where people phone with problems. I'd also save more, 150 a month, by giving up my weekend trips. And I'd do a short evening course on HR and employment law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On edge. It's like when the lift at work makes a strange noise: it's probably fine but you walk down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change first in the payroll team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The self-checkouts again. They'd put in a till scanner and my dad would keep doing what he does, which is knowing every customer's name. Honestly the shop has been the safe one: people go there for the chat as much as the rice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents' shop do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two senior ones would stay. Mrs Grewal because she knows the rules and the union. Gareth in the middle because he'd know how to make the system work. I'm the cheapest to cut, and I know it. I'd want to be seen as the person who helps people, not the person who types.

say: I'd say workers must be **involved** from the start and told what's changing.
I'd say it's like self-checkouts: they didn't close the shops but **changed** the jobs.
think: Payroll is thinking work with **fixed rules**, so it's exactly what software does.
Four of us pay 900 people, and it could be **two** of us in three years.
do: Learn the new system better than anyone and **train** the others.
Ask to move toward **employee relations**, where people phone with problems.
Take a short evening course on **HR** and employment law.
feel: **On edge**, like hearing a strange noise from the lift at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not something any one factory can solve. At work I'd say we need to look after each other, because the company might not. At the temple I'd say to the elders that the young are going to need real help, and that the community is where it starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm very worried. Payroll is mostly checking and rules, so it's among the first to go. I think I'd be out of the team within two years, and my cousins' jobs might go too. The family shop is the only thing that won't change quickly, and it can only support so many people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my manager and ask what the company plans, then look for work that has a person in it, like a care home's finance office. I'd cut costs hard: no more takeaways, use the bus not the car share. I'd work more at my parents' shop, perhaps full time if it came to that, and learn to run it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, and a bit guilty, because I'd be asking my parents for help after they've done everything for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How soon would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, probably the same Sunday. I'd go round after lunch and tell my mum first. She'd go quiet, then she'd say we'll manage, which is her way. My dad would ask what the plan is, and I'd have to have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shop help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would take me in, yes. My parents' shop doesn't pay much, but it's a floor. Right now it supports my parents and my uncle, and another full-time person means we'd all be on less. I'd learn to run it, then maybe improve it, with a delivery service and online ordering.

say: I'd say no one factory can solve this, so we must **look after each other**.
I'd tell the temple elders the young will need real **community** help.
think: Payroll is checking and rules, so I'd be out of the team within **two years**.
The family shop is the one thing that won't change quickly but can only support **so many**.
do: Ask my manager what the company plans and look for **care home** finance roles.
Cut costs hard and work more at my parents' **shop**, full time if needed.
Learn to **run the shop** properly and add online ordering.
feel: **Heavy** and a bit guilty, asking my parents for help after all they've done.
S2.quote: My parents' shop doesn't pay much, but it's a floor.
fieldNote: She has a real **fallback**: her family's shop, which she knows and helps with.
Guilt about asking for help is stronger than fear for herself.
She plans to improve the shop with online ordering, not just rely on it.

steps.text: Ask my manager what the company plans for payroll

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and that the company and the temple should help people learn new things. At work I'd say it's better to plan than to panic. At home I'd say be sensible and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a bit more hopeful. By 2031 I could have a real cushion, a bit of experience in employee relations and a better role. Sure, the date still comes, but I'd have time to turn from payroll to something with people in it, which feels like the safest thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the HR course in the first year and aim for an HR assistant job. I'd save 200 a month and keep the weekend shop hours. I'd also use more AI at work, so I'm known as the person who gets the best out of it, and I'd keep an eye on what the shop would need if I had to step in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a calm that I'd probably not trust fully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do five years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both of them work in similar offices, one in logistics and one in insurance. I'd tell them to start making themselves useful to people, not just to systems. Sit with the customers, learn the problem, do the thing that needs a conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that I'd get on with it. I'm good at slow, steady progress, which is perfect for five years. That's less good for two. I'd use the time to build trust at work and a bit of money in the bank.

say: I'd say five years is a fair **warning**, so plan and don't panic.
I'd say the company and the temple should help people **learn** new things.
think: By 2031 I could have a real **cushion** and experience in employee relations.
Turning from payroll to work with **people** in it feels the safest.

S3.quote: I'm good at slow, steady progress, which is perfect for five years.
fieldNote: Five years suits her **steady** nature, and she names that herself.

steps.text: Finish the HR course and apply for an HR assistant job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's ten years of time and we should use it well. At work I'd say let's keep learning. At home I'd say it's not something to be scared of. I'd probably say a prayer of thanks too, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm pretty calm. By 2036 I'd be 32, perhaps married, with the loan gone and maybe a share of the shop. My main risk is that I'm steady in a way that turns into slow. I'd need someone to tell me when it's time to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work toward a senior HR or finance role at the factory or another firm, clear the loan within eight years, and put savings into the shop's online side. I'd also learn how to use AI properly, with one course a year. And I'd try to buy a small house with my husband, if I have one by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit proud, like looking at a long garden path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what does your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A senior job in HR, a modest house, family close by. I'd be helping my parents retire the way they'd like to. I'd still go to the shop on Saturdays, probably for the company as much as the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm fine, and she should stop worrying. She'd say worry is how a mother loves, and I'd let her. It's good to be reminded that someone's thinking about you, even if it's a little too much.

say: I'd say it's ten years of time and we should **use it well**.
I'd say it's not something to be **scared** of, and thank God quietly.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32 with the loan **gone** and maybe a share of the shop.
My risk is being steady in a way that turns into **slow**.

feel: **Calm** and a little proud, like looking along a long garden path.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it comes before I can pay off the loan or build a cushion. What would help is companies telling us early, training that doesn't cost us our savings, and communities like my temple helping people stay together. I'd be fine if my parents' shop could carry us for a bit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that the first in the family to go to university carries a lot. Everyone's pleased, and you can't say you're scared. I'd like it to be okay to say that out loud.

headlineQuote: The first in the family to go to university carries a lot. Everyone's pleased, and you can't say you're scared.
portrait: Hana is a **22-year-old** payroll clerk at a Coventry car-parts factory, with a big loan and under a month of savings.
She's traditional, close to her family and temple, and works Saturdays in her parents' grocery shop doing the books.
She's steady: she tries new tools once they're proven, learns patiently and moves toward people-facing work.
She feels the pressure of being first in the family at university, and says that's the hardest thing to talk about.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because it comes before she can clear the loan or build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Early **warning** from companies, training that doesn't eat her savings, and family and community that can carry her briefly.
